studies.title: The Question They Keep Asking
studies.meaning: The surah opens by overhearing rather than addressing. A question is asked about a question: what is it they keep asking one another about. The answer names the subject only as the great announcement, the thing they are split over, and defines it no further. Most classical commentators read it as the resurrection, some as the Quran itself, and the sources record both readings. Then the reply arrives twice in identical words, and it withholds the information entirely.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, from a stage when the message had circulated far enough in the city to be argued about rather than ignored. No specific occasion is reported for these ayat. What the commentators describe is a public quarrel in progress: a claim passing from person to person, positions hardening around it, and the matter being treated as the news of the season rather than as something anyone intended to settle.

keyTerms.note: A reciprocal form, so the asking travels back and forth between people rather than being put to anyone able to answer. The verb pictures a rumour circulating, not an inquiry being made.
Arabic reserves this word for news that carries consequences, unlike the ordinary term for a report. Naming the subject with it concedes the event's importance before any argument about it begins.

The form describes people who have already sorted themselves into camps, not people who are merely uncertain. It says the disagreement had organised itself before anyone had a way of checking the claim.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca ran on talk. Caravans arrived carrying news and left carrying more of it, and the assemblies near the sanctuary existed partly as a market for it. A claim that the dead would be raised and sorted was exactly the kind of item that travelled well: short enough to repeat, impossible to test on the spot, and useful for holding an audience through a long evening.
studies.didYouKnow: The reply comes twice in identical words, with one particle meaning then added the second time and nothing else changed. From the sixth ayah to the last, thirty-five closing words in a row end on the same long vowel. The five that open the surah do not share it, so the sound changes exactly where the dispute stops and the evidence begins.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage answers a question by declining to answer it. Nothing about the great announcement is described here, only that knowledge of it is coming and will arrive as experience rather than as argument. That moves the dispute into a different category from the ones people are used to: not one where more debate produces more certainty, but one where the certainty has a date.

crossReferences.why: Names the same subject as tremendous news that the listeners are turning away from, using the same Arabic word.
Repeats a short warning clause word for word with a single particle added, exactly as these ayat do.
Quotes the denial of resurrection in their own words, then shows the moment it is corrected by sight.

studies.applyIt: Notice the next time an argument you are inside has stopped being about finding out. Watch for the point where both sides begin repeating positions instead of testing them. You do not have to win it, and you do not have to walk away. Just name it to yourself, quietly, and see whether it is still going anywhere afterwards.

studies.title: A Cradle, Pegs, A Covering
studies.meaning: The reply to the dispute is not an argument about resurrection but an inventory of things already done. It opens as a question with a negative inside it, which in Arabic asserts rather than asks, and then the verbs continue in the plain past. Earth as a cradle, mountains as pegs, human beings made in pairs, sleep as a severing, night as clothing. Nothing is proved here. Familiar facts are arranged until a further act of making stops sounding unlikely.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, addressed to listeners who have just been described as split over the great announcement. The commentators read the whole sequence from here to the sixteenth ayah as the ground of the answer rather than the answer itself, since the reply proper has been withheld twice. No occasion is reported. What frames the passage is a city that accepted the making of the world without difficulty and refused its remaking.

keyTerms.note: The word covers both an infant's cradle and a bed smoothed out for sleeping. It describes the earth by what it is prepared for rather than by what it is made of, and the Quran applies it to the earth three times.
The pegs that hold a tent's ropes into the ground. For people who struck camp regularly the image was not decorative: a peg is small, driven deep, and the only thing between a tent and the wind.
From a root meaning to sever or interrupt. Sleep is named as a nightly break in activity rather than as refreshment, which is why the commentators connect the word to a small rehearsal of dying.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A tent stands only as long as its pegs hold. Anyone who had travelled with a caravan had driven them in at dusk and pulled them out before dawn, and had seen what a night wind does to a peg set in loose sand. Earth spread flat enough to lie on, and mountains fixed hard enough to hold, were the two conditions of sleeping outdoors at all.
studies.didYouKnow: Sleep is called a severing in only one other place in the Quran, and there it sits beside night as a covering, exactly as here, though in the reverse order. The other passage completes the set with the day, as this surah does in its next line, but calls the day a revival rather than a livelihood.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Creation is presented here as provision rather than as display. Every item named is something a human being uses: ground to lie on, mountains that steady it, a partner, a break from consciousness, darkness to hide in. The argument for a second making is therefore built out of care rather than out of power, which is a different claim. The one who arranged all this is not finished.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same word for sleep as a severing and the same image of night as a covering.
Calls the earth a cradle in the same word, and draws from it a conclusion about guidance rather than resurrection.
Runs a longer inventory of the same kind, listing tents, wool, shade and garments as a completed favour.

studies.applyIt: Tonight, before you lie down, notice the two things this passage names as gifts: a flat place to put your body and a darkness you did not have to make. Neither is something you arranged. You will spend the next hours unconscious while something keeps running without you. Let that be the last thought rather than the day's unfinished list.

studies.title: Water Wrung From The Clouds
studies.meaning: The list moves from the ground upward and then back down. Day is named by what it is for rather than by its light: a time of getting a living. Above it seven strong things are built and a lamp is set burning among them. Then water comes down in quantity, and the sequence closes on grain, plants and thick gardens. The argument is a circuit rather than a catalogue, since everything sent from above is traced to something the listener eats.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The passage belongs to the long answer standing between the opening dispute and the naming of the Day of Sorting, and the commentators treat it as evidence gathered from what the audience could see for themselves. No occasion is reported for it. Mecca had no river and no rainfall it could count on; the trade routes around it existed partly because the valley could not feed itself from its own ground.

keyTerms.note: Formed from the verb to live, on a pattern that makes a place or time for doing something. Day is defined by the work done in it rather than by daylight, which is a claim about purpose.
An active participle from a root about squeezing or wringing out. The clouds are named as the thing doing the pressing, so the water is described as extracted rather than as merely falling.
An intensive form for liquid arriving in volume and without pause. Arabic has quieter words for rain; this one describes a downpour heavy enough to be heard from inside a tent.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Rain in the Hijaz arrives rarely and hard. A watercourse dry for a year runs within an hour, and seed waiting in the gravel comes up in days. Grain was carried in from the north or grown where such water gathered, so a heavy sky was watched with something close to arithmetic. Everyone in the valley could estimate how many months a single storm had just bought them.
studies.didYouKnow: Four of the five rhyme words in this passage occur nowhere else in the Quran: the term for livelihood, the adjective for the seven strong ones, the word for the blazing lamp, and the one for water pouring down. Only the fifth, vegetation, is used elsewhere. The surah is reaching for rare vocabulary to hold a single rhyme across thirty-five lines.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage makes the sky a working part of the economy rather than a decoration above it. Light is called a lamp, which is a household object, and rain is described as pressed out of clouds for the purpose of producing grain. That places God in the ordinary supply chain the listener already depends on, so denying the reckoning means denying the reliability of the same hand that fills the granary.

crossReferences.why: Sends down blessed water for gardens and grain, then names the resurrection as the same act repeated.
Asks directly who brings down the water and points out it could have been made bitter instead.
Also calls the seven heavens a structure and the sun a lamp, in nearly the same two images.

studies.applyIt: Find out where the water in your tap actually comes from, the reservoir or the river, and how far it travelled. It will take you five minutes. The passage names a supply line the listener could see from the doorway; yours is longer and hidden, which makes it easier to drink for forty years without once wondering who arranged it.

studies.title: The Appointment Already Fixed
studies.meaning: The gardens close the list of favours, and then the sentence changes register in a single line: the Day of Sorting has been fixed as an appointment. Everything after that is passive. The trumpet is blown, you arrive in crowds, the sky is opened and becomes doorways, the mountains are set moving and become a mirage. Nobody acts in these lines except by being acted upon, and the two things a listener treats as permanent, sky and mountain, are the two that go.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah has spent eleven ayat on what was made, and now names the day it withheld at the start, calling it the Day of Sorting rather than the Day of Judgement. That name is concentrated in this part of the Quran, and the surah placed immediately before this one turns on it. No specific occasion is reported. The audience is the same one described in the opening as split over the news.

keyTerms.note: Built from the word for time with a prefix that makes a fixed point, the same form used for the stated times of the pilgrimage. It names a scheduled thing rather than an eventual one.

A plural of the word for a band of people travelling together. It suggests arrival in separate groups rather than as one mass, which is why commentators connect it to communities coming forward one after another.

The shimmer that looks like standing water on hot ground. Applied to mountains it reverses the usual illusion: instead of nothing appearing to be something, the most solid thing in view turns out to be nothing.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A mirage was not a metaphor to anyone crossing open ground in summer. It is the standard hazard of the Arabian midday, a sheet of what looks like water lying across the plain, pulling a thirsty man off his line of travel. Guides knew it and warned against it, and every caravan carried someone who had once been fooled. A mountain dissolving into one would have landed as a remembered disappointment.
studies.didYouKnow: The Day of Sorting is named six times in the Quran, and three of those are in the surah placed immediately before this one, where the phrase is asked about and then answered. The word for mirage occurs only here and in one other passage, which uses it of the deeds of those who reject faith rather than of mountains.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Naming the day an appointment settles the question the surah opened with, without describing the day at all. What was in dispute was whether it would happen; the reply is that a time has been set. The passive verbs then strip every agent out of the scene except the one who is not named, so the dismantling of the sky reads as an act rather than as a catastrophe. A schedule implies someone keeping it.

crossReferences.why: Asks which day the matter has been deferred to and answers with the same name, the Day of Sorting.
Uses the mirage for the deeds of those who reject faith, water that vanishes when the thirsty reach it.
Answers a question about the mountains by saying they will be crumbled and the ground left without rise or dip.

studies.applyIt: Pick something you treat as fixed: a job, a body, a building you walk past daily. Give it thirty seconds and try to hold both facts at once, that it is solid and that it has an end you cannot date. Do not force a conclusion out of it. The passage does not draw one either; it only names the appointment.

studies.title: Lying In Wait
studies.meaning: The fire is described first by a posture rather than by heat. It is an ambush, something positioned along a road and waiting for people who are already travelling. Then it is called a destination for those who overstepped, using the ordinary word for the place a traveller is heading. Duration is given in long indefinite stretches, and the last two lines withhold the two things a desert traveller asks for, coolness and something to drink, before naming what is served instead.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah has just fixed the Day of Sorting as an appointment, and now sets out the two outcomes in turn, the harder one first, over ten ayat. No occasion is reported for these lines. The commentators note that the audience being addressed had heard the warning long enough to have stopped taking it as news, which is why the passage describes a place rather than repeating a threat.

keyTerms.note: The word for a place where a watcher lies concealed along a route. It occurs once in the Quran. Commentators differ over whether the fire waits for travellers or whether the road simply passes it.
A plural of a word for an extended stretch of time whose length was already disputed by the earliest scholars. The plural piles the stretches on one another without ever stating a total.
Classical readings run from intense cold to a dark fluid that seeps. The Quran uses it twice, both times beside the word for scalding water, so the pair covers the two ends of what a drink can be.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Raiding parties worked from ambush. A narrow place between hills, a bend where a wadi turned, a stand of rock above a well: these were known positions, and a caravan master planned a route by which of them he could avoid. Being watched from ground you had to cross was an ordinary anxiety, not a literary one. So was arriving somewhere and finding the water undrinkable.
studies.didYouKnow: Three of the five closing words in this passage occur nowhere else in the Quran: the one for the ambush, the one for the long ages, and the participle describing those who stay. The word for what is served to drink appears only twice in the whole Book, and in both places it stands beside the same word for scalding water.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Consequence is described here as terrain rather than as an event. Something has been positioned on a road that people are walking anyway, which makes the outcome a matter of direction rather than of a sentence handed down later. The passage also refuses to state a duration, giving stretches instead of a number, so hope and fear are both left without a figure to hold on to.

crossReferences.why: Says that your Lord is in a lookout post, using the same rare word from the other side of the image.
Names the same two drinks together, scalding water and the freezing draught, in the only other place.
Describes a scorching wind and boiling water, and denies coolness in almost the same construction.

studies.applyIt: Think about the roads you actually travel: the routine you keep, the arguments you return to, the hour of the evening you always lose. An ambush is placed where the traffic already is. Name one of those routes today, without deciding anything about it yet. Simply knowing which stretch of your week is exposed is most of the work.

studies.title: A Requital That Matches
studies.meaning: One word explains the whole preceding scene: the recompense corresponds. Then the correspondence is spelled out from the other end. They were not expecting a reckoning, and they denied the signs with an intensity the Arabic marks by doubling the verb's shape. Against that stands a single line saying everything has been counted in writing. The last ayah turns to direct address and gives the only imperative in the passage, and it is not an instruction but a verdict.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. These ayat close the account of the fire begun five lines earlier by explaining it rather than extending it. No occasion is reported. The commentators point out that the charge here is not the worship of idols, which the surah never mentions, but the refusal to anticipate any accounting at all, which was the settled attitude the early Meccan surahs meet most often.

keyTerms.note: From a root about two things fitting together or agreeing. It occurs once in the Quran. The word makes the outcome a match to the act rather than a penalty chosen to be severe enough.
The verb covers both hoping for something and reckoning that it may come. Used with a negative, it says they had no working expectation of an accounting, not merely that they denied one in argument.
An intensive verbal noun, rare in this form. It describes denial pursued as a practice rather than a single refusal, and the same form returns near the end of the surah in a very different setting.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Meccan trade ran on accounts. Goods went north on credit, shares in a caravan were tracked, debts were carried across seasons, and a merchant who could not produce his figures lost more than money. Writing existed mainly for exactly this: not literature, but records. Saying that everything had been enumerated in writing borrowed the most trusted instrument the audience had and applied it to their own conduct.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for a matching recompense occurs only here in the whole Quran. The clause saying that everything has been enumerated appears in one other place, where the enumeration is kept in a clear register and the subject is what people sent ahead of them along with the traces they left behind.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Justice is defined here as proportion rather than as force. The recompense is said to correspond, which rules out both excess and arbitrariness, and the ground for it is a record kept in advance rather than a judgement improvised at the end. What is being answered is not the crime of disbelief in the abstract but a specific failure of expectation: living as though nothing would ever be totalled.

crossReferences.why: Contains the only other statement that everything has been enumerated, there in a clear register.
Shows the record produced and the reaction to it, a book that has left out nothing small or large.
Sets the unit of the reckoning at the smallest weight there is, in two matching lines.

studies.applyIt: Keep an actual written record of one thing for a week: what you spend, what you say to one person, how you use an hour you usually lose. Not to judge it, only to see it written. The passage puts weight on enumeration rather than on memory, and a week of your own figures will show you why the two are not the same.

studies.title: Where Nothing False Is Heard
studies.meaning: The turn is marked by a single word meaning a place of winning through, set against the ambush a few lines earlier. Four short items follow, walled gardens, vines, well-matched companions and a cup filled to the brim, each given in two words or less. Then the description stops naming pleasures and names an absence instead: no empty talk there, and no lying. The list ends on what the ear will not have to hear rather than on what anyone will have.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The passage answers the ten ayat before it point for point, and the commentators read the two panels as deliberately unequal in length, the account of the fire being the longer. No occasion is reported. The audience had been told that the reckoning was matched to the deed; this is the other half of that statement, and it arrives without any transition at all.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning both to succeed and to get clear of danger. It occurs once in the Quran and carries the second sense alongside the first, so the reward is also described as a getting away.
Said of a vessel poured to the very rim. The word appears once in the Quran, and commentators note it implies continuous refilling as much as a single generous pour.
Speech with no content or consequence, including the loose oath a person does not mean. Naming it as absent treats a conversation without weight as itself a thing worth being spared.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A cup that never came up short mattered in a place where hospitality was the measure of a man and water was rationed by the day. So did the walled garden, which in Arabia meant a plot with a wall around it and a share in a spring, the rarest kind of property there was. And an assembly free of idle talk described something the tribal councils, where reputations were made and destroyed by speech, were not.
studies.didYouKnow: The description of the garden closes on the word for lying, and it is the same intensive form used seven ayat earlier for the denial that put people in the fire. The surah takes the word that named the offence and places it, negated, among the rewards. Two of the four items here are also words that occur nowhere else in the Quran.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The final item is the one that carries the argument. Paradise is defined not only by what is supplied but by what is subtracted, and the thing subtracted is bad speech. That makes the reward partly social rather than only sensory, and it answers a surah that opened with people questioning one another in a dispute nobody could settle. The end of the arguing is itself part of what is promised.

crossReferences.why: Also promises a place where no idle talk is heard, and gives the one word spoken there instead.
Ends its account of the garden the same way, on a place where no empty speech is heard.
Names the same absence of idle talk and adds provision arriving morning and evening.

studies.applyIt: Sit through one conversation today without adding anything that has no weight: no filler complaint, no repeating of news you have not checked, no joke at someone's expense. You will notice how much of the usual air it removes. The passage treats being spared that kind of talk as a reward, which is worth testing for an hour before you decide whether it is one.

studies.title: A Gift, And No Reply
studies.meaning: Three words describe the reward and they pull in different directions. It is a recompense, which is earned, and then a gift, which is not, and then a word that scholars read either as ample and sufficient or as calculated against what was done. The sources record the range without settling it. The next line then widens from the reward to its giver, listing His domain, naming Him the Most Merciful, and closing with a denial: nothing there has any right of address to Him.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The two ayat stand at the hinge where the surah stops describing outcomes and turns to the one who assigns them. The commentators note that the name chosen at this point is the Merciful rather than a name of power, in a sentence that is otherwise about how far above address He stands. No occasion is reported for these lines.

keyTerms.note: A giving with no obligation behind it. Set immediately after the word for recompense, it corrects the accounting sense of the sentence: what arrives is more than the arithmetic would have produced.
The same word used earlier in the surah for the accounting they did not expect. Here scholars read it as sufficient and abundant, or as measured out against deeds, and the tradition preserves both.
Not speech in general but the act of speaking to a person, the word used of a formal address. Denying it says that nothing on that day has standing to open a conversation, let alone to argue.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Access to a chief was the whole of political life. A man with a grievance needed someone to speak for him, a tie of kinship or a formal protection, before he could put a case at all. Standing in front of a ruler you had no claim on, with nobody to introduce you, was the ordinary shape of powerlessness. The line about address describes that, and removes even the intermediary.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for a reckoning appears twice in this surah and nowhere else in it: once of the accounting the deniers were not expecting, and once here as the measure of the gift given to the righteous. The name the Most Merciful also appears twice, in this ayah and the next, and not once in the thirty-six lines before them.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage refuses to let reward settle into either of the two available ideas. Called a recompense, it looks earned; called a gift, it looks unearned; and the third word keeps both readings open. Then the giver is described by a name of mercy in the same breath as an absolute limit on approach, which holds nearness and distance together rather than choosing. Mercy here is not familiarity.

crossReferences.why: Adds a further increase beyond everything the people of the garden could want, the same movement past the earned.
Also restricts speech on that day to whoever the Merciful permits, with the same pairing of mercy and limit.
Says that on the day it comes no soul will speak except by His leave, in one short clause.

studies.applyIt: Think about the last thing you were given that you had not earned and could not have arranged. Not a general blessing, a specific one, with a date. Sit with the fact that no arithmetic explains it. Most people find they have to look further back than they expected before they find one, which is itself worth noticing today.

studies.title: Standing In A Single Row
studies.meaning: The scene is silence held by rank. The Spirit and the angels stand in one row, and even they do not speak unless permission is given, and whoever is permitted says only what is correct. Scholars differ over what the Spirit is here, reading it as Gabriel, as an angel of the highest order, or as a created order of its own, and the sources record the range. Then one line changes the subject completely and offers the listener a way back.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah is closing, and the last two ayat move from the assembled ranks of that day to a decision available on this one. The commentators treat the offer at the end as the point the whole chapter has been building toward, since the opening dispute is answered not by information but by an open door. No occasion is reported for these ayat.

keyTerms.note: Named separately from the angels and placed before them. Classical readings include Gabriel, a great angel, and a distinct order of creation, and the commentators record the range without deciding among them.

One line rather than a crowd, the same word used of ranks drawn up for battle and of worshippers standing shoulder to shoulder. It describes order imposed from outside, not a gathering that arranged itself.
From a verb meaning to come back. The same word appeared earlier in this surah for where those who overstepped end up, so the two destinations are named with one term.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: In a tribal assembly the right to speak was the whole hierarchy made visible. Order of speaking followed age, lineage and standing, and a younger man who spoke out of turn was corrected on the spot. Deputations to a chief waited outside until called. A row of the highest beings in creation waiting for permission would have read as an image of protocol, drawn from something everyone present had stood in.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for a place of return occurs twice in this surah, once of the destination waiting for those who overstepped and once here of the way back to one's Lord. The same noun does both jobs. The surah also uses a word for what the permitted speaker says that appears nowhere else in the Quran.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage sets an absolute constraint and then immediately opens a door. Nothing in creation, including the highest ranks of it, can speak unbidden; and the very next line hands a human being a choice, phrased as whoever wills. Freedom is granted at the point where the scene has just shown how little standing anyone has, which places the offer entirely on the side of what is given rather than what is owed.

crossReferences.why: Also names the Spirit alongside the angels descending, keeping the same distinction between them.
Has the ranks speak for themselves, saying that each has a known station and stands in rows.
Closes a warning with the identical offer, that whoever wills may take a way to his Lord.

studies.applyIt: Notice today how often you speak because there is a gap rather than because you have something correct to add. Try one meeting or one meal where you wait to be asked. The passage puts the highest ranks of creation in a silence they hold until permitted, and the discipline transfers downward more usefully than it sounds.

studies.title: I Wish I Were Dust
studies.meaning: The surah's last ayah states the warning plainly and then dates it: the punishment is near. What follows is one image and one sentence of speech. A person looks at what his own hands have sent ahead, and the looking is the whole event; nothing is read out to him. Then the one who rejected faith speaks, and what he says is not a plea or a defence. It is a wish to have been something that was never accountable at all.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The chapter began with people asking one another about a piece of news and ends by telling them what the news is and how close. The commentators note the shift to direct address in the closing line, after a surah that has mostly described. No occasion is reported. What the wording assumes is an audience that treated the warning as remote, which is the assumption the word for near is placed against.

keyTerms.note: Warning of a specific danger, distinct from the general word for giving news. This exact form, with the direct object attached, occurs once in the Quran, and it puts the whole surah into the category of notice given.
The verb for sending something on ahead of you rather than for doing it and leaving it behind. Deeds are pictured as already at the destination, waiting, which changes what a person is looking at.

The ordinary word for the dust of the ground, and the material the Quran repeatedly names as the origin of the human being. Wishing to be it is a wish to go back below the point where responsibility started.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Dust was what a caravan raised, what settled on everything in the valley, and what a body was returned to in a shallow grave scraped out of stony ground. It was also the cheapest thing in Arabia, worth nothing and belonging to nobody. A man of standing in Mecca measuring his life against a handful of it would have been saying something exact about status, not only about escape.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase for wishing something had been otherwise occurs seven times in the Quran, and each carries a different wish: to have been with them, not to have associated anything with God, to have died before, to have taken a path with the messenger, not to have been handed the record, to have sent something ahead for one's life. Only here does someone wish to be dust.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The final wish identifies exactly what is unbearable, and it is not the punishment. It is having been the kind of creature whose acts count. Wanting to be dust is wanting the dignity withdrawn, which makes accountability itself the thing that has become intolerable. The passage lets that stand as the closing line of the surah, without comment, so the value of being answerable is argued from the wish to be rid of it.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same phrase for what a person's hands sent ahead, but there it is forgotten rather than seen.
Carries another of the seven wishes, this one for having sent something forward for one's life.
Also has a person informed of what he sent ahead and what he left behind, on the same day.

studies.applyIt: Name one thing you did this week that is now out of your hands and already arrived somewhere: a message sent, money given, something said to a child. You cannot revise it. Rather than judging it, just practise the grammar of the ayah for a moment, and think of that act as ahead of you rather than behind you.
